title: Jubilee (Leviticus 25)
hook: every fiftieth year debts forgiven and land returned; the Church still keeps holy years

segments.voice: Yesterday, be holy: holiness in wheat fields, wages and the corners of a field. Your line was leave the corners.

In Philadelphia there's a cracked bell, the Liberty Bell, with a line of scripture around its top about proclaiming liberty throughout all the land. It's from Leviticus twenty-five. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, words it differently: "proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land." Liberty or remission, the verse wasn't first about a nation's independence. It was about a year. A strange, radical year that came around once every half century.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `PROCLAIM LIBERTY.` → `ONCE EVERY HALF CENTURY.`

segments.voice: First, the count. Every seventh year in Israel was a sabbath for the land: no planting, the fields rest. Count seven of those, forty-nine years, and the fiftieth is the jubilee. It begins on the Day of Atonement with a blast on the ram's horn through the whole land. The year's Hebrew name, yovel, is traditionally linked to that ram's horn, and it's where the word jubilee comes from. Second, what happens. Land a family sold in hard times goes back to them. People who sold themselves into service for debt go free and return to their families. The land rests again. And God gives the reason: the land is mine, and you are strangers and guests with me. Third, the honest question. Did Israel ever fully keep it? The sources are mostly silent, and scholars still debate it. But the idea never went away. When Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, he read from Isaiah about the acceptable year of the Lord, and some readers hear in it the language of jubilee. Fourth, the Catholic holy year. In 1300, Pope Boniface the Eighth proclaimed the first Christian jubilee, a year of pilgrimage and forgiveness in Rome. The Church still keeps them, opening holy doors in Rome that stay sealed between jubilees. Before the year 2000, Pope John Paul the Second called for the debts of the poorest nations to be reduced or forgiven, a jubilee for whole countries. And some word historians think the Latin heard yovel alongside iubilare, to shout for joy, which may be why our word sounds like joy.
screen: `SEVEN SEVENS, THEN THE FIFTIETH.` · `YOVEL: THE RAM'S HORN SOUNDS.` · `LAND RETURNS, DEBTORS GO FREE.` · `HOLY YEARS AND HOLY DOORS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing someone owes you: twenty dollars never paid back, an apology you're still waiting for, a favor you keep score of. Picture writing it off, the horn sounding and the slate clearing; you don't have to tell them, you just stop collecting. If you pray, you can say the line from the Our Father as Matthew gives it: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors"; if not, picture the ledger closing.
Jubilee. From yovel, the ram's horn: the fiftieth year, when land returned and debtors went free. The Church still keeps holy years. Today's word.
Your line: a year to set free. Every fifty years, the count started over. Day three hundred eighty-three, in the books.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church proclaims ordinary jubilee years, when pilgrims pass through the holy doors of Rome's major basilicas and seek reconciliation, and popes have also called extraordinary jubilees, such as the Year of Mercy.

notes: Leviticus 25:10 quoted from the KJV because that is the wording on the Liberty Bell; the DR reads differently ('proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land'). Confirm the choice for the Catholic path.
Liberty Bell named by abolitionists (1830s): commonly stated; confirm.
Whether the jubilee was historically observed is debated; stated plainly.
First jubilee proclaimed by Boniface VIII in 1300 (bull Antiquorum habet fida relatio); ordinary jubilees every 25 years since 1475; the 2025 Jubilee ('Pilgrims of Hope'). Confirm.
John Paul II's call for reducing or cancelling the international debt of poor nations: Tertio Millennio Adveniente 51. Confirm.
Yovel / iubilaeus / iubilare: standard etymology; confirm.
The practice quotes the Our Father in the Matthew form 'forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors' (Matthew 6:12); the Mass form uses 'trespasses'. Quoted from the DR; confirm wording.
